### **Session · What happened (July 28)**
The session on July 28 focused heavily on the architectural design of AI agents, particularly concerning prompt engineering, memory structures, and the judicious use of metadata for scoping conversations. Discussions highlighted the critical importance of understanding LLM behaviors, how to prevent hallucinations and repetitive responses, and the necessity of implementing guardrails to ensure responsible AI interactions. The team also reviewed the proper use of RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) and the differences between conversation history and retrieval in an AI system.

### **Technical concepts discussed**
- **Prompt Engineering and LLM Behavior**: Extensive discussion on how prompts dictate LLM output behavior, emphasizing the need for structured prompts (headings, bullet points) for better AI understanding. The mentor stressed that prompts literally determine every output behavior of an LLM [28 July 2026, Page 19-20 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Memory Structure (User-Scoped Conversations)**: Explored building memory structures for agents that are user-scoped, meaning conversations and transcripts are linked to a specific user ID via metadata. This ensures privacy and personalized retrieval of conversation history [28 July 2026, Page 10-11 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Metadata for Filtering and Scoping**: Clarified that metadata is crucial for filtering and scoping information, especially in multi-user agent systems. It can be used to scope by user ID, conversation ID, message ID, or chunk ID, enabling personalized retrieval and preventing data leakage between users [28 July 2026, Page 9-10 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Context Window and Token Limits**: Discussed the importance of understanding an LLM's context window and token limits, particularly when chunking documents for summarization. Giving all documents at once can lead to slow performance due to these limitations [28 July 2026, Page 3-4 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Guardrails and Anti-Hallucination**: Introduced the concept of guardrails to prevent AI from engaging in harmful or inappropriate behavior, especially in sensitive domains. Techniques for preventing LLM hallucinations and ensuring character ownership were also discussed [28 July 2026, Page 18-19 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Difference between Conversation History and Retrieval**: Siddharth explained that conversation history determines the flow of the current dialogue, while retrieval brings in broader, relevant information (e.g., historical documents or intelligence packages) that might span years [28 July 2026, Page 24 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Agent Design Principles**: Emphasized thinking about agents as "hired persons," defining their specific role, purpose, and scope of work using "first principles" thinking [28 July 2026, Page 7-8 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **LLM Model Understanding**: Highlighted the necessity of understanding the underlying LLM model (e.g., its training data, parameter count like Lama 3.18B having 8 billion parameters) as it impacts performance and capabilities [28 July 2026, Page 3-4 — Siddharth Saminathan].

### **Assignments and actions**
- **Himaya Perumal**:
    - Define the role, purpose, and uniqueness of each agent (Manager, Mentor, Team) and present must-haves, could-haves, and should-haves for all three agents. Consider the implications of re-embedding if user scoping is not currently in the metadata [28 July 2026, Page 13-14 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    - Think about how to prevent information sharing between users if only one agent is used for teammates [28 July 2026, Page 7-8 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    - Continue experiments related to context window and chunking [28 July 2026, Page 15 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Dakshinya Nachimuthu**:
    - Read about LLM API call batching, retries, and context engineering. Implement these concepts to improve summarization performance, potentially trying with the DeepSeek model if current performance is slow [28 July 2026, Page 3-4 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    - Continue experiments related to context window and chunking [28 July 2026, Page 15 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Team-Wide Action**:
    - Read about RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) [28 July 2026, Page 15 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    - Read about "working pre" and understand related concepts (specific execution for today, reading tomorrow) [28 July 2026, Page 3-4 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    - Sit and write out detailed prompt instructions, considering emotional handling, safety checks, and loop-breaker rules, even if an AI tool formalizes it later [28 July 2026, Page 20-22 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    - Develop "first principles" thinking for agent design, considering the scope and job of each agent as if "hiring" them [28 July 2026, Page 7-8 — Siddharth Saminathan].
    - Review the file on context window and prompt for the last time [28 July 2026, Page 17 — Siddharth Saminathan].

### **Decisions**
- **Agent Memory Scoping**: It was decided that agent memory (conversation transcripts) should be user-scoped using metadata to ensure privacy and personalized information retrieval [28 July 2026, Page 10-11 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Metadata for Filtering**: Metadata will be used for compulsory filtering based on user ID to retrieve relevant information in multi-user scenarios [28 July 2026, Page 10-11 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Single Agent for Teammates**: The approach of using a single agent for teammates was questioned due to privacy concerns regarding exposing individual performance data. The team needs to address how to ensure information doesn't share between teammates if they use the same agent [28 July 2026, Page 7 — Siddharth Saminathan].

### **Important changes**
- **Embedding Strategy**: If multiple agents are pursued, re-embedding everything will likely be necessary if user scoping is not currently included in the metadata [28 July 2026, Page 13-14 — Siddharth Saminathan].
- **Prompt Structure for LLMs**: The emphasis shifted to highly structured and detailed prompts, moving beyond simple system instructions to include micro-instructions for input handling, response deduplication, call handling, and even emotional guidance, to precisely control LLM behavior and prevent undesirable outputs like hallucination or gaslighting [28 July 2026, Page 19-20 — Siddharth Saminathan, 28 July 2026, Page 20-22 — Siddharth Saminathan].
